blocks.text: Which sometimes swells heifers, sometimes pot-bellied calves. And in the Theriaca on the haemorrhous, line 306:
Τῆς γὰρ ὀδαξομένης τὰ μὲν ἀθροὰ πίμπραται οὖλα, [Tēs gar odaxomenēs ta men athroa pimpratai oula,]

When she bites, the whole gums swell, or else burn. For so the Scholiast: Πίμπραται· ὑποκαίεται, καὶ πυροῦται [Pimpratai; hypokaietai, kai pyroutai]. And a little later: Πυρακτοῦνται, καὶ ἀναβράζουσι [Pyraktountai, kai anabrazousi]. Nor is it taken otherwise in Lucian, when he says of the dipsas, πίμπρασθαι ποιεῖ [pimprasthai poiei]. For there follows: Καὶ βοῶσιν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν πυρὶ κείμενοι [Kai boōsin hōsper hoi en pyri keimenoi]; And they (who have been bitten) cry out like those who lie in fire. In Luke, therefore, it can be rendered either way. Accordingly one of the Arabic versions has here: They expected that he would يحترق [yaḥtariq] burn. And Castalio: as they expected that he would burn. But Jerome: They supposed that he would be turned into a swelling, that is, that he would swell up. Arias and Beza follow this, and many other more recent writers. And not without reason, since among the symptoms that follow the bite of a viper this is one of the chief and most conspicuous: the bitten part swells at once. Dioscorides, book 6: Τοῖς δὲ ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθεῖσιν οἰδεῖ, καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἱκανὸν τὸ σῶμα ξηραίνεται [Tois de hypo echidnēs dēchtheisin oidei, kai eph᾽ hikanon to sōma xērainetai]; In those bitten by a viper the body swells and dries up severely. Nicander, where he treats of those bitten by a viper, Theriaca, line 240:

— — — φλύκταιναι ἀραιαὶ, Οἷα πυρικμήτοιο χροὸς, κλαδόωσιν ὕπερθεν· [phlyktainai araiai, Hoia pyrikmētoio chroos, kladoōsin hyperthen;] [III, 147] harmful swellings boil up on the surface, as if the body had been burnt with fire. So also Paul of Aegina: Pustules break out on the bitten part, as in burns. And Aëtius writes that from a wound inflicted by a viper there arises a bilious, hot, blistered, reddish swelling, etc. And Avicenna, in the chapter On the bite of vipers, at the foot of p. 137: ثم يظهر ورم حار احمر ذو بثور كثيرة ونفاطات كحرق النار [thumma yaẓhar waram ḥārr aḥmar dhū buthūr kathīra wa-nuffāṭāt ka-ḥarq al-nār] Then there appears a hot, red swelling, full of many blisters and pustules, as from burning by fire. These indeed agree. But against what is found at the end of the same chapter, واكثر ما يهلك يهلك في ثلثة ايام وربما بقي الي السابع [wa-akthar mā yahlik yahlik fī thalātha ayyām wa-rubbamā baqiya ilā al-sābiʿ] Most of those who perish, perish on the third day, and sometimes they survive until the seventh, it seems possible to object that the Maltese thought that Paul, bitten by the viper, would fall down dead on the spot, as though sudden death followed a viper's bite. I reply that according to Aëtius τοὺς ἐχιοδήκτους [tous echiodēktous] mostly die within seven hours. And in Pliny, book 11, chapter 53, the arrows of the Scythians, dipped in viper's gore, bring death at once by a light touch (though in the Mirabilia of Aristotle one reads only μιγνύουσι τῷ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰχῶρι, καὶ οὕτω ποιοῦσι θανάσιμον [mignyousi tō tēs echidnēs ichōri, kai houtō poiousi thanasimon].). And in Pausanias' Boeotica a certain Phoenician relates ἄνθρωπον ἀποφεύγοντα ὁρμὴν ἔχεως, ἐπί τι ἀναδραμεῖν δένδρον, τὸν δὲ ἔχιν. ὡς ἦλθεν ὕστερος, ἀποπνεῦσαι πρὸς τὸ δένδρον τοῦ ἰοῦ, καὶ οὐ ζῆν ἔτι τὸν ἄνθρωπον [anthrōpon apopheugonta hormēn echeōs, epi ti anadramein dendron, ton de echin. hōs ēlthen hysteros, apopneusai pros to dendron tou iou, kai ou zēn eti ton anthrōpon], that a man, to escape the attack of a viper pursuing him, took refuge in swift flight up a certain tree; when the viper came there a little later, it breathed its poison upon the tree, and the man ceased to live. So among the Arabs جارية [jāriya] giaria is a kind of viper that kills at once. Hence Damir, in the Proverbs on the viper: رماه الله بافعي جارية وهي التي يموت لذيعها من ساعته [ramāhu Allāh bi-afʿā jāriya wa-hiya allatī yamūt ladhīʿuhā min sāʿatihi] God has cast him to a giaria viper, that is, has thrown him into an incurable evil: because whoever is bitten by this viper dies that very moment. For a viper's bite is more deadly according to its place [col. 375] or food, and if it bites when hungry, and in summer days, and when it has first been provoked. For then, with its bile inflamed, the poison becomes much sharper. Moreover, some bodies, and some parts within bodies, resist poison less. Since, then, there are so many causes why vipers kill by their bite either more slowly or more quickly, the time of the coming death cannot be fixed with certainty. But the viper that had attacked Paul could seem to have a most potent poison, because it had burst out of the midst of the fire more agitated and roused. So since a speedy death was feared from its bite, and the barbarians had waited a long time, and no harm had come to Paul, μεταβαλλόμενοι ἔλεγον Θεὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι [metaballomenoi elegon Theon auton einai], changing their minds they said he was a god, whom they had previously judged to be a murderer. Indeed, [III, 148] The rustic brood knows no measure.
While fools avoid vices, they run into the opposite ones.

As Paul was not a murderer, so neither was he a god, but a most faithful servant of God. Before, they sinned gravely against charity; now against faith. For, as Oecumenius notes, the gentiles were accustomed πάντα ποιοῦντά τι παράδοξον Θεὸν νομίζειν [panta poiounta ti paradoxon Theon nomizein], to take for a god anyone who performed something marvellous. Thus the people of Lystra decreed divine honours to this same Paul because he had healed a lame man; but a little later the same people stoned him: Act. XIV, 10. 19.
